priorInvolvementDisclosure: I returned ACCEPT on v17 at 0/0 and Codex returned REJECT with HAE17-CX-01. Codex is right. That is my fifth under-call and my second consecutive wrong ACCEPT, and the honest conclusion is that my method had a specific systematic hole rather than that I was careless once. At v17 I declared I would test what each governing rule permits by constructing counterexamples rather than checking that today's data conforms. I then constructed counterexamples only for the two attacks Codex had already published, confirmed the new rule rejected them, and certified. My counterexample testing was retrospective, not generative. The clause Codex attacked, 'A file that matches neither extracts the empty set', is one I read and quoted approvingly in my own v17 measurements as 'a selection order and an empty-set fallback are stated', without once asking what input reaches it. Codex generates novel probes against fresh text; I was replaying known ones. The change I fixed before reading v18 was to enumerate each governing rule's branches and, for every branch, ask what input reaches it and yields a permissive result, treating every fallback, default, otherwise, empty, skip or unrecognized clause as fail-open until the text proves otherwise. I wrote ten probes of my own construction against the v18 extractor, of which three are novel rather than replays, and the finding below came from those three. The opposite guard also still applies: two wrong ACCEPTs create pressure to reject this one to compensate, and I tested the finding against that by asking whether I would raise it had I already found something else. I would.

shouldFix.title: The severity-array branch still silently discards a severity key that is neither an object array nor an integer, and the empty-extraction guard catches this only when no other key supplied ids
evidence: The extraction clause is typed narrowly. severityArrays.ids reads 'concatenate object.id from blockers[], then shouldFix[], then advisories[], for each key that is an array of objects'. A key that is not an array of objects contributes nothing and the rule states no refusal for it.

The refusal clause covers only one of the non-conforming types. integerCountCrossCheck refuses when 'a positive integer count on a skipped key' is present. A skipped key that is an object, a string, or an array of non-objects is neither an array of objects nor an integer count, so no clause reaches it.

I constructed three probes of my own and ran them against the rule implemented as written. blockers=[{id:X}] with shouldFix={'count':2} extracts ['X']; with shouldFix='2' extracts ['X']; with shouldFix=[1,2] extracts ['X']. In each case any findings the malformed key represents are erased with no refusal and no mismatch.

The guard that would otherwise catch this fires inconsistently. emptyExtraction requires, for the severity branch, that 'every present severity key is either an empty object array or integer 0'. With blockers=[] and advisories=[] and shouldFix={} the extraction is empty, that condition fails, and the rule correctly REFUSES. With blockers=[{id:X}] and the identical malformed shouldFix={'count':2} the extraction is non-empty, emptyExtraction never engages, and the same malformation passes. Protection against a given malformed key therefore depends on whether an unrelated key happened to yield an id.

This is the third member of the enumeration the repair addressed rather than a new class. HAE17-CX-01 named two silent-loss paths, the unrecognized whole-file schema and the skipped positive integer count. v18 hardened both, the first to 'unrecognized schema and REFUSES; it MUST NOT extract the empty set' and the second explicitly, and left the remaining per-key type unaddressed.

The live corpus is sound, which bounds this to SHOULD-FIX. I implemented the v18 extractor exactly as written and ran it over all fourteen pinned verdict lanes for v8 through v17: zero refusals, zero set mismatches, 56 (lane, id) pairs equal in both directions, and 28 FromVN prefixes equal to the 28 REPAIRED register ids. Both of Codex's original probes are now correctly refused.
shouldFix.impact: frozenReviewFindingExtractor and registerCoverageRule are declared GOVERNING and exist so that findings cannot be silently lost from the lineage check; registerCoverageRule.resultIfIncomplete says the successor refuses. A frozen verdict whose severity key is emitted as an object, a string, or an array of scalars, which is exactly what a partial or version-skewed writer produces, has its findings erased with the check reporting complete. That reopens the omission class the rule was introduced to close, and it does so through the same clause the previous round repaired, which is the one-sided-repair pattern this lineage has produced at v9, v11, v13, v14 and v15.
shouldFix.requiredRepair: Make the severity branch total over key types rather than over one type. Refuse whenever a present severity key is neither an array of objects nor an integer count, so object, string and array-of-scalar shapes fail closed exactly as the unrecognized whole-file schema now does. Equivalently, state that every present severity key MUST be an array of objects or an integer count and that any other shape REFUSES, and make emptyExtraction's key-shape condition apply to every extraction rather than only to empty ones, so the guard no longer depends on whether a sibling key produced ids.

advisories.title: The combined-branch integer cross-check is ambiguous when no integer count is present, and the strict reading refuses a conforming file
advisories.observation: The clause opens 'For each of blockers/shouldFix/advisories that is an integer count:' and then requires that 'the extracted id count MUST equal the sum of those integer counts (absent integers contribute 0)'. Two readings follow. Under the strict reading the comparison always runs, so a combined-schema file carrying findings=[{X},{Y}] and no integer count fields at all sums to 0, mismatches 2, and refuses. Under the scoped reading the comparison engages only when at least one integer count is present, and the same file passes. I ran the strict reading against the corpus and it has no live effect: all three combined-schema files carry counts that reconcile exactly, v8 claude2 at 0 findings with blockers 0 and advisories 0, v10 claude2 at 4 with 2+2+0, and v12 claude2 at 3 with 1+2+0.
advisories.whyNotShouldFix: The ambiguity errs fail-closed. The strict reading refuses a conforming file rather than admitting a malformed one, so it cannot silently lose findings, which is the property the rule exists to protect. No corpus file is affected and no claim the artifact makes is false. Recorded because a rule declared GOVERNING and offered as a mechanical check should not admit two readings that disagree on a conforming input.
advisories.suggestedDisposition: Optional. State whether the comparison engages when no integer count is present, for example by adding that a combined-schema file with no integer count fields skips the cross-check and extracts normally.

advisories.title: Three advisory subjects remain substantively unaddressed from v11 through v18
advisories.observation: FC-SUBTYPE-CLASS still exercises no CA-3 row despite CA-3 carrying the largest subtype domain including the deferred KEYCHAIN; destinations.actionSubtype still mixes record and serialized class vocabulary in its requiredness clause before restating it serialized; coveredActs still keys the host classes as CA-1-host-head and CA-4-host against the record vocabulary. Both reviewers have raised all three across seven generations, most recently as HAE17-ADV-01/02/03, all correctly registered ADVISORY-NON-BLOCKING and correctly absent from the repair arrays.
advisories.whyNotShouldFix: The merits are unchanged: the subtype binding is stated normatively in three places and only the fixture population is short, the mapping sentence is immediately restated unambiguously, and the coveredActs keys are labels rather than discriminator literals. I have declined to escalate these at v13, v15, v16 and v17 and nothing in v18 alters their consequence.
advisories.suggestedDisposition: Optional. One CA-3 accept row and one CA-3 cross-class refuse row would close the first at negligible cost.

verdictBasis: The dispatch permits ACCEPT only at 0 blockers and 0 SHOULD-FIX. This review returns 0 blockers and 1 SHOULD-FIX, so the verdict is REJECT. Both claimed repairs largely land: Codex's two silent-loss paths are closed and I verified that by implementing the rule as written and re-running his frozen probes, and my own v17 advisory is adopted with the repair-array namespace anchored so the mis-ingestion that tripped my tooling cannot recur. Custody is clean on every pin, all 55 recorded inputs reproduce, the corpus passes the stated rule across fourteen lanes with 56 matching pairs and a 28-to-28 FromVN correspondence, and no prior repair regressed. The finding comes from the method change I committed to before reading the subject: rather than replaying Codex's probes, I enumerated the extractor's branches and constructed seven of my own. Three of them show that a severity key emitted as an object, a string, or an array of scalars is skipped with no refusal, erasing whatever findings it represents, and that the empty-extraction guard catches that malformation only when no sibling key supplied an id. That is the third member of the enumeration HAE17-CX-01 addressed, in the same clause, with the same consequence for a rule whose stated purpose is that findings cannot be silently lost. The live data is sound, which is why it is SHOULD-FIX rather than a blocker, and one clause closes it.
